EICMA 2026 • Yamaha Births New Adventure Scooter Family, Three RW Models That Look More Like Motorcycles
15-YO Pizza Boy Got a '69 Mach 1 in 1983, Made It Into a Wheelie-Popping Racer, Beat His Own Shelby
65 photos
Photo: Facebook/Shelby Thurman
In 1905, Gennaro Lombardi popularized coal-oven pies on Spring Street in Manhattan, establishing Lombardi's as the landmark widely celebrated as America's first pizzeria, selling whole pies for 5 cents. Simultaneously in Detroit, Ford Motor Company was building its 1905 lineup, led by the $2,000 four-cylinder Model B, the $1,000 Model F touring phaeton, and the $950 opposed-twin 10-hp Model C capable of a brisk 30 mph.
Nobody in 1905 expected a Ford to haul mozzarella across town at felony velocities. Dedicated American pizza delivery did not truly arrive until around 1950, pioneered by trailblazers like Casa D'Amore in Los Angeles and Pizza King in Dallas. By the 1960s, suburban sprawl, television dinners, and Domino's Pizza—founded in 1960 with its famous 30-minute delivery guarantee—cemented doorstep pizza delivery as an unmistakable pillar of American popular culture.
Decades later, one Tennessee teenager took that 30-minute promise personally and turned it into the world's fastest pepperoni shuttle. Meet Steve Thurman of Portland, Tennessee, as he tells his story to Erik Larsen on the Heart and Horsepower YouTube channel. Needing extra cash after washing cars at Baker Motor Company, a Buick dealership in Gallatin, Thurman moonlit at Domino's, delivering hot pies in a roaring 1969 Ford Mustang Mach 1 .
Delivering pies in a classic Mustang beat flipping burgers by a mile, especially once Thurman memorized every Friday and Saturday regular. Spotting an order for the Jones family, he blasted straight to their porch in record time, pocketed a generous tip, and promptly hijacked his leftover minutes on the clock to cruise town with his buddies. Rolling back into Domino's, his amazed coworkers heard the same cheeky report: delivered early, paid well, no problem.
Photo: Facebook/Shelby Thurman Today, that former teenage delivery rocket looks less like a salami courier and more like a blacked-out menace itching for a green light. Wearing glossy black paint, “Steve Thurman Performance” door lettering, and a pinned matte-black scoop hood, the 1969 Mach 1 sits on massive Phoenix F/X slicks beneath back-halfed quarters. Behind the firewall, the cabin is completely stripped, outfitted with Lexan windows, gutted doors, a full roll cage, racing gauges, and an electronic delay box.
Even Thurman's pre-run ritual drips with deadpan drag-strip humor. Popping the hood exposes a gleaming mechanical fuel injection hat that racers lovingly call "the toilet," which he dutifully wipes clean with a rag before flipping the fuel switch. Waking the barn in Portland with a violent, ground-shaking lope, the bar-less Mach 1 refuses to even contemplate traction on cold garage concrete, casually blowing its oversized slicks off before it ever sees a starting line.
Remarkably, Thurman has owned this Mustang continuously since 1983, a 43-year saga sparked by a lucky family trade at age 15. Back then, young Steve owned a gutted 1965 Mustang mid-restoration that his father desperately wanted, while his uncle parked this running blue 1969 Mach 1 in his driveway. Jumping at the swap, Steve added wheels, tires, an interior, and a stereo, roaring into high school the instant he turned 16 with a legitimate hot rod.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower To appreciate what Thurman carved into a drag warrior, consider the towering heritage behind the galloping pony badge. Debuting in April 1964, the Ford Mustang invented the affordable American pony car and triggered a showroom stampede that has now spanned seven distinct generations. Sales-wise, nothing ever matched the original first generation built from 1964½ through 1973, which moved an astounding 2,981,259 units in the United States—peaking at 607,500 cars in 1966 alone.
By 1969, Ford gave the first-generation Mustang a wider, longer-hooded restyling and cranked out 299,824 units across three core body styles. Hardtop coupes led the charge with 150,640 built, encompassing standard, deluxe, bench-seat, and 22,182 luxury Grandé trims. Open-air convertibles were scarce at just 14,746 units, while the sleek SportsRoof fastback accounted for 134,438 cars—highlighted by 72,458 newly introduced Mach 1 models alongside 1,628 Boss 302 and 857 Boss 429 homologation specials.
Engine choices in 1969 epitomized Detroit excess, spanning ten configurations from 115 hp to 375 hp. Buyers picked 200- or 250-cubic-inch sixes (115 hp and 155 hp), a 302 V8 (220 hp), 351 Windsor V8s (250 hp and 290 hp), a 390 V8 (320 hp, 10,464 built), 428 Cobra Jet V8s (335 hp, 13,261 built), or the homologation Boss 302 (290 hp) and Boss 429 (375 hp).
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower Three transmissions backed those motors: a standard 3-speed manual, an optional 4-speed manual required on both Boss models, and the 4-speed Select-Shift Cruise-O-Matic automatic—pairing the C4 with smaller engines and the C6 with big-blocks. As a Mach 1, Thurman's car originally packed Ford's standard 351-cubic-inch Windsor V8, factory-rated at 250 hp (in two-barrel form) or 290 hp (with the four-barrel carb).
Following his drag-racing father's footsteps, Thurman began uncapping headers and bolting on slicks, soon winning his very first night after wiring in a delay box. That winter, buddy Rodney McCall back-halfed the chassis and welded the cage—back when nobody panicked about cutting up a 1969 Mustang . Today, that original stock 351 block is stroked to 414 cubic inches with an Eagle crank, Eagle rods, Mahle pistons, Trick Flow heads, and methanol-fed Enderle injection.
Burning methanol keeps the stroker cool and dead consistent through muggy Tennessee summers without even needing a cooling fan. Power flows through a trans-brake BTE Powerglide and BTE converter to a 9-inch Ford rear end packing steep 5.14 gears, controlled by four-corner double-adjustable shocks that Thurman dialed in himself.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower Before those adjustable shocks arrived, the fresh 414 staged a terrifyingly funny stunt at Bowling Green. Launching hard, the Mach 1 hiked its nose skyward and stayed airborne even after shifting gears automatically. Peeking sideways at half-track without wheelie bars, a rattled Thurman tapped the brakes, landing in a shower of sparks past his stunned rival.
Today, it carries controlled wheelies past 60 feet—right after Thurman's favorite part, a roaring line-lock burnout. And that’s only because Steve is taking it easy – on the car, on himself, on the sport itself. If he really buried his foot in it, and pulled all the stops on the car, his Mach 1 would do a quarter-mile run perfectly vertical, headlights pointing straight at the sky. No wheelie bars, as we can plainly see in the video.
More than iron and methanol, this Mustang anchors a generational Blue Ova l obsession. Thurman's passion for Ford never stopped at the drag strip, the garage, or even the realm of automobiles—he literally named his daughter Shelby, stamping Mustang royalty straight onto the family tree. During the Heart and Horsepower shoot, Steve uncovered a 20-year-old photograph of baby Shelby beaming inside the Mach 1, and she happily climbed back in to recreate the exact pose.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower Their bond shines brightest at the strip, where father and daughter trade friendly smack talk as rivals. Representing Team Music City against Shelby's Team Ethridge, they staggered staging lanes to avoid meeting early, only to clash in the finals—where Steve took bragging rights after an eager Shelby red-lighted. Probably the most bitter-sweet victory of his career.
Ask if he would ever sell the Mach 1, and Steve refuses flatly: Shelby would kill him, because someday, the world's fastest pizza car is hers. After all, she’s known this amazing machine her whole life (she’s 21), and there’s now way in heaven that she’s letting go of it.
